title: Ambien and Alcohol: Why Zolpidem and Drinking Don't Mix
excerpt: Why Ambien (zolpidem) and alcohol shouldn't be mixed: how both slow the brain, the FDA boxed warning on sleep-driving, Lunesta and Sonata, how long to wait, and emergency signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Ambien? How zolpidem and alcohol stack up in the brain, the FDA sleep-driving warning, Lunesta risks, how long to wait, and danger signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't take Ambien (zolpidem) on a night you've been drinking. Both alcohol and zolpidem slow down the brain through the same chemical "brake" system, so together they add up to more sedation, more memory loss, and more risk of doing things in your sleep that you won't remember. The Ambien medication guide tells patients not to take it if they drank alcohol that evening or before bed. That's not a technicality. Many of the worst outcomes linked to zolpidem, including sleep-driving, involve alcohol on top of the pill.

**The quick rules:** If you've had a drink tonight, skip the Ambien and accept a worse night of sleep instead. Never use alcohol to help a sleeping pill "kick in." Only take zolpidem when you can stay in bed for a full 7 to 8 hours. If you take it most nights and like to have a drink in the evening, ask your prescriber exactly what's safe for you, because the answer depends on your dose, your age, and which version you take. If someone took Ambien and alcohol and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist** about alcohol and any sleep medicine you take. This article explains general research and drug-label guidance, not your personal situation. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has taken Ambien (or an unknown sleeping pill) and alcohol can't be woken, is breathing slowly or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips, or is vomiting while barely conscious. **Call your doctor soon if** you've done anything in your sleep you don't remember (eating, texting, driving, leaving the house), you feel groggy or unsteady the morning after a dose, or you want to stop zolpidem after taking it for weeks or longer. For a possible overdose, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## How Ambien and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Ambien is a brand name. The drug inside it is **zolpidem**, a prescription sleep medicine. Doctors often call it a "Z-drug," along with eszopiclone (Lunesta) and zaleplon (Sonata). Zolpidem comes in a few forms: regular Ambien, extended-release Ambien CR, and tablets that dissolve under the tongue.

### Both work on the brain's GABA system

Your brain has a built-in calming signal called **GABA**. When GABA binds to its main receptor (the GABA-A receptor), nerve cells quiet down. That's the brain's brake pedal.

- **Zolpidem** binds to GABA-A receptors and makes them respond more strongly to GABA. It's fairly selective for the receptor types tied to sleep, which is why it's prescribed for insomnia.
- **Alcohol** also boosts GABA-A signaling, among other effects on the brain. That's a large part of why a few drinks make you relaxed, uncoordinated, and sleepy. Our guide to [alcohol and GABA](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-gaba) explains this in more depth.

When you take both, you're pressing the same brake pedal twice. The effects don't simply sit side by side. They stack, and the result can be much more sedation than either would cause alone. This is called an **additive** effect, and for some people it behaves more like multiplication than addition.

### What that stacking looks like in real life

- **Deeper, harder-to-reverse sedation.** You may be far more out of it than you expect, and harder to wake.
- **Slower breathing.** At normal doses in healthy people, zolpidem alone has little effect on breathing. Add alcohol, a higher dose, an opioid, or untreated sleep apnea, and the risk of breathing that's dangerously slow or shallow goes up.
- **Memory blanks.** Both alcohol and zolpidem can block new memories from forming. Together, a short "I don't remember going to bed" can become hours you can't account for.
- **Poor coordination and falls.** Getting up to use the bathroom in the night is a common moment for falls and injuries, especially in older adults.
- **Complex sleep behaviors.** This is the risk that sets the Z-drugs apart, and it gets its own section below.

### The timing problem

Zolpidem works fast. Most people feel it within 15 to 30 minutes, which is why the label says to take it right before bed. The regular version has a short half-life, meaning the body clears about half of it in roughly two to three hours in a typical healthy adult. Alcohol, meanwhile, stays in your system for hours after your last drink. Your body clears about one standard drink per hour, but that's a rough average with a lot of variation.

So if you drink at dinner and take Ambien at 11 pm, the alcohol is very often still in your blood when the zolpidem peaks. That overlap is exactly what the label warns against.

## What the FDA and the Ambien Label Say

This isn't an area of guesswork. US regulators have taken several steps on zolpidem and its relatives.

**The label says not to combine them.** The Ambien medication guide tells patients not to take it with alcohol, and not to take it if they drank alcohol that evening or before bed. The prescribing information warns that alcohol and other drugs that slow the brain (central nervous system depressants) add to zolpidem's effects, including next-day impairment.

**A boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors (2019).** In 2019 the FDA added a boxed warning, its most prominent kind, to zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon. It covers "complex sleep behaviors": sleepwalking, sleep-driving, and doing other activities while not fully awake. The FDA said these events had led to serious injuries and deaths, and that they can happen after just one dose, even in people who had never had a problem before. People who have had a complex sleep behavior on one of these drugs should not take it again.

**Lower doses for women (2013).** In 2013 the FDA cut the recommended starting dose of zolpidem for women in half: from 10 mg to 5 mg for immediate-release, and from 12.5 mg to 6.25 mg for extended-release. The reason was that women clear zolpidem more slowly, so more of it is still in the blood the next morning, enough to impair driving and other activities that need alertness. The FDA advised prescribers to consider the lower dose for men too.

**A "full night" rule.** The label says to take zolpidem only if you can stay in bed for a full night (7 to 8 hours) before you need to be active again. Taking it late, or on a night you'll be up early, raises the odds of next-morning grogginess. Alcohol makes that worse.

**It's a controlled substance.** Zolpidem is a Schedule IV drug in the US, meaning it carries some risk of misuse and dependence. That's part of why it's usually meant for short-term use.

## Complex Sleep Behaviors: Why Alcohol Makes Them More Likely

This is the risk most people have heard about, sometimes as a joke. It isn't funny when it happens.

"Complex sleep behaviors" means doing things that look purposeful while you're not actually awake. Reported examples include:

- Getting up and walking around, sometimes leaving the house
- Eating, sometimes large amounts or odd things, or cooking
- Making phone calls, sending texts, or posting online
- **Driving a car** ("sleep-driving")
- Having sex

The person usually has no memory of it afterward. Some of the serious events reported to the FDA involved falls, burns, near-drownings, exposure to cold, car crashes, and deaths.

These behaviors can happen with zolpidem alone, at normal doses. But the older prescribing information specifically noted that alcohol and other brain-slowing drugs appeared to raise the risk, and that taking more than the prescribed dose did too. In real-world reports of sleep-driving, alcohol is a recurring factor. That makes sense: alcohol lowers judgment, deepens amnesia, and adds to the sedation, so the half-awake state lasts longer and runs deeper.

**What to do if it happens to you:** stop taking the medicine and call your prescriber. Don't just try to "be careful next time." The label says people who've had one of these episodes shouldn't take the drug again.

**A practical safety step:** if you take zolpidem, keep car keys somewhere that takes effort to reach at night, and don't take it in a hotel or unfamiliar place after a night out.

## Zolpidem and Alcohol: Does the Version Matter?

People search for "zolpidem and alcohol" as often as "Ambien and alcohol." They're the same drug, so the same rules apply to every brand and generic. But the version you take changes how long the overlap risk lasts.

| Version | How it works | What it means with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Regular zolpidem (Ambien, generics) | Fast-acting, short half-life of roughly 2 to 3 hours in typical adults | Strongest overlap risk if you drank that evening. Usually mostly cleared by morning in healthy adults, but not always. |
| Extended-release (Ambien CR) | A two-layer tablet that releases some drug right away and more later | Effects last longer into the night and next morning. Next-day impairment is more likely, especially with alcohol in the picture. |
| Dissolving tablets (under the tongue) | Absorbed faster through the mouth | Same alcohol warning. Some low-dose versions are made for middle-of-the-night waking and require hours left in bed before getting up. |

A few groups clear zolpidem more slowly and should be extra careful about both the pill and alcohol: **women**, **older adults**, and **people with liver problems**. Liver disease matters twice here, because the liver handles both zolpidem and alcohol.

## Lunesta and Alcohol (and Sonata)

**Lunesta** is the brand name for **eszopiclone**, another Z-drug. It works on the same GABA-A system as zolpidem, and its label carries the same boxed warning about complex sleep behaviors and the same advice not to drink alcohol with it.

The main difference is how long it lasts. Eszopiclone has a longer half-life than zolpidem, roughly six hours in healthy adults. That means more of it is still in your body the next morning. In 2014 the FDA lowered the recommended starting dose of Lunesta to 1 mg after studies found that the 3 mg dose could impair driving, memory, and coordination the next day, even when people felt fully awake. Adding alcohol the night before only adds to that.

**Sonata** (zaleplon) is the shortest-acting of the three, with a half-life of about an hour. A short half-life doesn't make it safe with alcohol. The peak effect, when alcohol and the drug overlap, is the dangerous part, and Sonata carries the same boxed warning.

The practical takeaway is identical for all three: **if you drank tonight, skip it tonight.**

## "I Already Took Ambien After Drinking. What Now?"

This happens. If you or someone you're with took zolpidem after drinking, here's a sensible way to handle it.

**If it was a normal prescribed dose and a drink or two, and the person is awake and making sense:**

- Don't take any more of anything: no second pill, no more alcohol, no other sleep aid or antihistamine.
- Go to bed and stay there. Don't drive, cook, take a bath, or go outside.
- If you're with someone else, let them know what you took so they can check on you.
- In the morning, don't drive until you feel fully alert, and give it extra time. You may be more impaired than you feel.

**Call 911 or get emergency care right away if the person:**

- Can't be woken, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, irregularly, or with long pauses
- Has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
- Is vomiting while barely conscious (turn them on their side so they don't choke)
- Took more than the prescribed dose, took other sedatives or opioids too, or drank heavily

While you wait, keep them on their side and stay with them. Don't leave someone alone to "sleep it off" if you're worried. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to watch for in more detail.

## How Long Should You Wait Between Ambien and Alcohol?

There's no official waiting period that fits everyone. Anyone who gives you an exact number of hours is guessing. Here's what you can say with confidence.

**Drinking first, then Ambien:** the label's guidance is simple. If you drank that evening or before bed, don't take it that night. That's the clearest rule available, and it's the one to follow.

**Ambien first, then drinking the next day:** for most healthy adults on regular immediate-release zolpidem, the drug is largely cleared by the next afternoon or evening. But "largely cleared" isn't the same for everyone. Women, older adults, people on extended-release versions or Lunesta, and people with liver problems can have the drug in their system longer. If you take zolpidem regularly and want to know whether a glass of wine with dinner the next evening is okay, that's a perfect question for your prescriber or pharmacist, because they can look at your dose and your full medication list.

**Never drink while it's working.** Drinking after taking zolpidem, even something small "to fall asleep faster," is the worst version of the combination.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from Ambien and alcohol together if you:

- **Are over 65.** Older adults clear zolpidem more slowly and are more prone to confusion, falls, and hip fractures. The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a widely used guide for prescribing to older adults, recommends avoiding Z-drugs in older people for these reasons.
- **Are a woman**, because zolpidem tends to stay in the blood longer.
- **Have sleep apnea or lung disease.** Both alcohol and sedatives relax the airway and can worsen breathing pauses at night. See our guide to [alcohol and sleep apnea](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-sleep-apnea).
- **Have liver disease**, which slows how quickly you clear both substances.
- **Take other brain-slowing medicines**, such as opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines like [Xanax](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol), muscle relaxants, gabapentin, sedating antidepressants such as [trazodone](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol), or sedating antihistamines. Each one adds another foot on the brake.
- **Have ever had a complex sleep behavior** or a memory blank on a sleeping pill.
- **Drink heavily on a regular basis**, which can change how your body handles sedatives and raises the stakes of every overlap.

If any of these apply, the "talk to your doctor" advice isn't a formality. Ask directly: "Is it ever okay for me to drink on a night I take this?"

## Why People Mix Them, and Better Options

Most people who end up combining Ambien and alcohol aren't being reckless. Usually it's one of these:

- **"I had a few drinks and now I can't sleep."** This is very common. Alcohol makes you drowsy at first, then breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night as your body processes it. People wake at 3 am wired and reach for a pill. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's happening and what helps.
- **"A nightcap helps me fall asleep, and the pill keeps me asleep."** Alcohol is a poor sleep aid. It shortens the time to fall asleep but suppresses REM sleep and leads to lighter, more broken sleep later. See [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) for the full picture.
- **Travel and jet lag.** A drink on the plane and a sleeping pill to adjust to a new time zone is a common and risky pairing. Pick one, not both, and talk to your doctor before the trip.

**If you've been drinking and can't sleep**, the safest choice is usually to skip the pill and ride it out. Get some water, keep the room dark and cool, put the phone down, and accept that tonight's sleep will be worse. A bad night is recoverable. An overdose or a sleep-driving crash may not be.

Be cautious with "safer" swaps too. Over-the-counter sleep aids like diphenhydramine (the antihistamine in many "PM" products) and doxylamine are also sedating and also add to alcohol's effects. Melatonin is far less sedating, but stacking sleep products on a night of drinking still isn't a great idea. See our guides to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) and [sleeping pills and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) for a side-by-side look at the options.

## Stopping Zolpidem: Don't Go Cold Turkey After Long-Term Use

If you've taken zolpidem most nights for weeks or months, stopping suddenly can cause rebound insomnia (sleep that's worse than before you started) and, less commonly, withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, shakiness, and in rare cases seizures. This is more likely at higher doses or after long use.

The fix isn't to keep taking it forever. It's to work with your prescriber on a gradual taper. Many people do well switching to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), a structured, talk-and-habits approach that sleep specialists recommend as a first-line treatment for long-term insomnia.

The same logic applies to alcohol. For social drinkers, this isn't a concern. But if you drink heavily every day and want to stop, sudden stopping can cause dangerous withdrawal, and it's worth doing with a doctor's help.

## Where DHM Fits In, and Where It Doesn't

We cover DHM (dihydromyricetin) a lot on this site, so it's worth being clear about it here.

DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol. A well-known 2012 animal study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication in rats and appeared to work partly through **GABA-A receptors**, the same receptor system zolpidem and alcohol act on. Human evidence is still limited.

That has two honest consequences:

1. **DHM does not make Ambien and alcohol safe together.** There is no good evidence that any supplement prevents the sedation, breathing, memory, or sleep-behavior risks described above. The core rule doesn't change: don't combine them.
2. **Don't add DHM to zolpidem without asking.** Because DHM seems to act at the same receptor system in animal studies, and its interaction with Z-drugs in people hasn't been studied, check with your prescriber or pharmacist before taking DHM if you take Ambien, Lunesta, or any other sleep medicine. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) goes into this further.

For social drinkers who **aren't** taking sleeping pills or other sedating medicines, DHM is one of the supplements people discuss alongside the basics: drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers the research. If you take zolpidem, though, that conversation belongs with your prescriber, and our [sleep aids and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) compares the other sleep medicines and how each one interacts with drinking.

## The Bottom Line

- Ambien (zolpidem) and alcohol both act on the brain's GABA "brake" system. Together they add up to deeper sedation, more memory loss, slower breathing, and a higher risk of sleepwalking, sleep-eating, and sleep-driving.
- The Ambien medication guide says not to take it if you drank alcohol that evening or before bed. Follow that.
- Lunesta (eszopiclone) and Sonata (zaleplon) carry the same boxed warning and the same alcohol advice. Lunesta lasts longer, so next-morning impairment is a bigger concern.
- Women, older adults, and people with sleep apnea, liver disease, or other sedating medicines are at higher risk.
- If you drank and can't sleep, skip the pill tonight. If someone is hard to wake or breathing slowly after mixing them, call 911.
- If you take zolpidem regularly and want to drink, ask your prescriber what's safe for you specifically.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Ambien?**

You shouldn't drink alcohol on a night you take Ambien. Both slow the brain through the same GABA system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, memory blanks, slowed breathing, and complex sleep behaviors like sleep-driving. The Ambien medication guide says not to take it if you drank alcohol that evening or before bed. If you take it regularly and want to know about drinking on other days, ask your prescriber.

**What happens if you take Ambien after drinking?**

The effects of the two stack. You may become much more sedated than expected, harder to wake, and more likely to have memory gaps or do things in your sleep you won't remember, such as eating, texting, or driving. Breathing can slow, especially at higher doses or with other sedatives. If you've taken a normal dose after a drink or two and feel okay, take nothing else, stay in bed, and don't drive in the morning until you're fully alert. If someone can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911.

**How long after drinking can I take Ambien?**

There's no official waiting period that fits everyone. The clearest guidance is from the label: don't take Ambien if you drank alcohol that evening or before bed. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot. The safest approach on a night you've been drinking is to skip the pill and accept a worse night of sleep.

**Is zolpidem and alcohol the same risk as Ambien and alcohol?**

Yes. Zolpidem is the drug inside Ambien, so generic zolpidem, Ambien, Ambien CR, and the dissolving tablets all carry the same alcohol warning. Extended-release versions last longer, which can make next-morning impairment more likely, especially if you drank the night before.

**Can you drink on Lunesta?**

No, not on a night you take it. Lunesta (eszopiclone) works on the same GABA system as Ambien and carries the same boxed warning about complex sleep behaviors. It also lasts longer in the body, with a half-life of about six hours, so next-day impairment is a bigger concern. The FDA lowered its recommended starting dose to 1 mg in 2014 because of next-morning effects on driving and memory.

**Why does Ambien have a boxed warning?**

In 2019 the FDA added a boxed warning to zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon about complex sleep behaviors: sleepwalking, sleep-driving, and doing other activities while not fully awake. These events led to serious injuries and deaths, and they can happen after a single dose. Alcohol and other sedatives appear to raise the risk. Anyone who has had one of these episodes should stop the medicine and call their prescriber.

**Can I drink the day after taking Ambien?**

For many healthy adults on regular immediate-release zolpidem, most of the drug has cleared by the next evening. But women, older adults, people with liver problems, and people on extended-release versions or Lunesta may have it in their system longer. Because the answer depends on your dose and health, ask your prescriber or pharmacist before planning to drink the day after a dose.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on Ambien?**

Check with your prescriber or pharmacist first. In animal studies DHM appears to act partly on GABA-A receptors, the same system zolpidem works on, and its interaction with Z-drugs in people hasn't been studied. There's also no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine Ambien and alcohol.
